newsitem.title: UK: Gilts end near lows as overseas interest dries up.
newsitem.headline: Gilts end near lows as overseas interest dries up.

text.p: 1620 GMT - Gilts ended near session lows on Friday having set yet another contract high earlier after U.S. PPI data landed surprisingly weak. Overseas interest in gilts, seen earlier in the week, evaporated. Focus next week on key retail sales figures. * March gilt settled 2/32 higher at 113-12
That gave the U.S. Treasuries market a healthy hue, leaving gilts to trail in its wake.
Underperformance was the name of the game for the gilt market. The 10-year spread over Bunds sidled out to 176 basis points, from 170 at the start of the session.
Adams said the gilt curve steepened in the process. "The long end of the curve has been offered."

Economists said the market is waiting with baited breath for an announcement of Britain's election date. Prime Minister John Major told Sky Television on Thursday he would not hold a vote later than May 1 but hinted he would not call one imminently.
But later comments from the Prime Minister muddied the waters again.
Peter Osler, economist at GNI, said the gilt curve would continue to steepen if Major holds out until May.

"If Major can hold out until his preferred date of May 1 it means probably only a 25 basis point rate rise by June. If policy stays unchanged while the economy is clearly strengthening the curve is going to steepen."
The gilt market will refocus on the interest rate debate on Monday when Bank of England Governor Eddie George and his deputy, Howard Davies, testify to the Treasury Select Committee.
This week, the Bank, in its quarterly inflation report, urged a modest tightening of monetary policy.
The June short sterling future settled one basis point higher at 93.48 on Friday, near to discounting a half-point increase in six base rates by the half-year stage.
On Wednesday, retail sales data for January will be released. After a shock 0.8 percent fall in December another weak figure would suggest consumers are certainly not on a spending spree.
Anecdotal evidence from the Confederation of British Industry and British Retail Consortium suggest sales were underwhelming again in January.
David Philpotts, economist at Schroders, forecast a modest 0.2 percent in January sales -- "only a partial rebound after a dismal pre-Christmas trading period."
But he said the underlying trend remained reasonably robust.
